Preprint. Work in progress.
SABREAGENT:
LANGUAGE MODELS AT DESIGN
TIME FOR LOST-SALES INVENTORY CONTROL
Yang Liu1, Yulin Huang1, Xue Yu1, Jiong Dong1, Jianshen Zhang1, Yongzhi Qi1†
1Supply Chain Tech Team Y, JD.com
†Corresponding author.
ABSTRACT
SabreAgent uses a language model at design time to construct two components
for lost-sales inventory control: a product-specific seasonal prior and a validation-
selected capped base-stock policy family. During operation, statistical forecast-
ing and inventory optimization use these frozen artifacts to determine orders, with
zero language-model calls. We evaluate the approach on the 1,320 instances of In-
ventoryBench. Under the benchmark’s cost assumptions, the operations-research
core draws on a zero-lead-time optimality result and a projected-inventory rule for
positive deterministic lead times. The latter computes replenishment shortfalls by
propagating inventory using sales along simulated demand paths. The seasonal
prior adds forecast variants alongside the original forecaster, and the selected pol-
icy family handles stochastic lead times with order destruction. SabreAgent scores
0.6311, compared with 0.5380 for the strongest published baseline, and ranks first
in all six benchmark cells. Ablations attribute most of the gain to the OR core. In
the paired analysis, the seasonal component adds 1.79% across the three real-data
cells, and the search component adds 2.3% across the two stochastic-lead-time
cells. These results demonstrate how model-generated priors and policy structure
can improve an OR controller through design-time use.
1
INTRODUCTION
InventoryBench gives each policy only five initial demand observations, while real instances also
provide product descriptions (Baek et al., 2026). Effective replenishment requires combining these
limited observations and seasonal cues with inventory costs and supply dynamics. Nine of the
benchmark’s ten published baselines consult a language model every period. Each resulting order
commits inventory before its outcome is observed. Work on planning and self-correction identifies
limitations of using generated reasoning to assess such decisions (Huang et al., 2024; Liu et al.,
2025).
Design-time use lets external procedures inspect and evaluate a model-generated policy, prior, or
representation before deployment. This division of labor underlies verifier-guided program search
(Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025) and the broader
“model proposes, verifier disposes” view (Kambhampati et al., 2024). Prior work in operations re-
search has used language models to formulate and translate optimization problems (Ramamonjison
et al., 2023; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2024). SabreAgent applies this division of la-
bor to inventory control, with statistical forecasting and optimization handling sequential decisions
during operation. Figure 1 illustrates this division of labor.
Across InventoryBench’s 1,320 lost-sales instances, all ten published baselines score below a hind-
sight diagnostic that chooses one constant order-up-to level per instance. This offline reference
motivates an explicit treatment of inventory costs and dynamics.
SabreAgent builds its control core from the benchmark’s cost structure. Orders have no purchase or
setup cost and leftover inventory has no salvage value. At zero lead time, some optimal post-order
inventory level is bounded above by max{It, y∗
t }, where y∗
t is the myopic critical-fractile level.
Under stationary demand, the myopic policy is optimal. For positive deterministic lead times, we

Figure 1: Two placements of language models in inventory control. (a) A model generates orders
inside the decision loop. (b) SabreAgent uses a frozen seasonal prior alongside the forecaster without
seasonal adjustment and a validation-selected policy family. Statistical forecasting and OR control
generate orders without runtime language-model calls.
project the committed pipeline through the lost-sales dynamics and price only the residual shortfall.
A textbook inventory-position target treats demand that was already lost as if it had depleted the
pipeline. For stochastic lead times, where an order may be destroyed, the policy instead evaluates a
small family of replenishment rules using the same simulated demand and supply trajectories.
The language model supplies two additions to this core. We elicit a normalized seasonal shape
from product descriptions and use it to construct additional forecast variants. The original fore-
caster without seasonal adjustment remains in the mixture; §3.3 gives the associated predictive-
loss bounds. An automated research loop also proposes policy families for the lossy-supply cells.
Scores on separately generated validation instances guide the selection of a capped base-stock fam-
ily. Building on established capped base-stock policies in lost-sales control (Xin, 2021), we link
the cap to destroyed-order catch-up bursts and combine design-time family selection with online,
instance-specific parameter search.
The final policy scores 0.6311, versus 0.5380 for the strongest published baseline, and leads in every
benchmark cell. The ablation separates the sources of this performance: the frozen OR core reaches
0.6180 on the batched evaluation path, and the two model-authored components add +0.0138 on
that same path. Paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero for the seasonal component on real-data cells
and the search component on stochastic-lead-time cells. A same-model online-adjustment control
adds bounded per-period order changes to the complete policy. On its 124-instance subset, the real
stochastic cell is the only cell with a positive estimate exceeding two standard errors.
The analysis and ablations identify the contributions of the cost-based control core, seasonal fore-
casting, and policy-family selection. Related work and proofs appear in the appendix.
2
PRELIMINARIES
2.1
CONTROL PROBLEM AND EVALUATION
Each InventoryBench instance (Baek et al., 2026) tracks one product at one location for T weeks,
with T = 50 for synthetic instances and 47 for real ones. Inventory starts at zero. The nonnegative
demand path dt is fixed by the instance, and unmet demand is lost (Zipkin, 2008a; Bijvank & Vis,
2


--- Page 3 ---
Preprint. Work in progress.
2011). In the benchmark’s own timing the policy first observes on-hand stock It, the in-transit
total Xt and the position IPt = It + Xt, all before that period’s arrivals are booked. It then
places qt ∈Z≥0, scheduled for t + Lt when Lt < ∞and destroyed otherwise. Arrivals At =
P
t′≤t qt′1{Lt′ < ∞, t′ + Lt′ = t} are added to stock next, the sum including t′ = t, so at L = 0
an order lands in the period that places it. Sales are st = min(dt, It + At), and holding is charged
on the ending inventory Iend

Costs are (p, h) ∈{(1, 1), (4, 1), (19, 1)}, so the critical ratio ρ = p/(p + h) is 0.50, 0.80 or 0.95,
all three present in every cell.
The policy receives a partial observation of the system state. Initially it receives five dated demand
observations, the promised lead time, p, h, and, for a real instance, a product description. In later
periods it sees the date, It, Xt, and the previous demand, order, and arrival, then maps the resulting
history Ht to qt. In-transit inventory is only a total; its age profile and the current realization of Lt
are hidden when the order is placed. Demand itself is uncensored, unlike the usual lost-sales setting
in which stockouts conceal the upper tail and couple learning to control (Huh & Rusmevichientong,
2009). No exploration term is therefore needed for demand estimation.
Two regimes set Lt to 0 or 4. The stochastic regime uses {1, 2, 3, ∞}; Lt = ∞denotes permanent
order destruction. The benchmark fixes one lead-time sequence per cell and shares it across that
cell’s instances. A policy is told only a promised lead time of 2 and must learn survival from
observed inventory movements. Because demand and supply paths are fixed during scoring, the
expectation in the policy’s planning objective is internal to its predictive model; the reported score is
computed on the realized benchmark path. Crossing two data sources with three lead-time regimes
gives the six cells in Table 7.
Each instance is scored by a normalized reward, and the headline number is its unweighted mean
over the 1,320 instances:

The denominator is the reward from serving every unit immediately with no ending inventory. It
is attainable with perfect demand information when L = 0. With positive lead time, however,
an empty initial system cannot serve demand before its first possible arrival, and destroyed orders
impose an additional loss. Thus NR = 1 is the ideal-service reference for normalization; §4.2
reports a supply-feasible clairvoyant diagnostic.
2.2
WHAT THE COST STRUCTURE IMPLIES
Purchase cost, fixed ordering cost, and salvage value are all zero in the benchmark. Inventory can
normally be valuable because it avoids a future purchase or setup cost (Scarf, 1960), or because it
covers demand that no future order can reach (Arrow et al., 1951; Zipkin, 2000; Porteus, 2002).
Under (1), a future order is free. At L = 0, it can also arrive in time to serve that period’s demand.
Carrying an extra unit therefore offers no saving on future orders and incurs h in each period it
remains unsold. The analysis takes p, h > 0, orders unbounded above, and demand exogenous,
nonnegative and independent across periods with known marginals.
Theorem 1 (zero-lead-time policy structure). Assume zero purchase, setup, and salvage costs and
L = 0. Let y∗
t be a ρ-fractile of period-t demand. Then Vt is non-increasing, and some optimal
post-order level is no greater than max{It, y∗
t }. Lookahead may reduce the myopic order but cannot
improve the value by increasing it. If the fractiles admit a non-decreasing selection over time—in
particular, under stationary demand—then Vt is constant on [0, y∗
t ] and the myopic policy yt =
max{It, y∗
t } is optimal.
The proof, integer-order extension, and a counterexample when fractiles fall over time appear in Ap-
pendix B. Classical work studies near-myopic behavior in broader inventory settings (Karlin, 1958;
Morton, 1971; Zipkin, 2008b). The exact statement here uses instantaneous, free replenishment.
Our positive lead-time heuristic applies the theorem’s cost intuition through a projected-inventory
surrogate.

Figure 2: SabreAgent’s two-stage architecture. (A) The frozen seasonal prior enters a forecast mix-
ture that retains the flat variant; the associated bounds concern predictive log loss. (B) Validation
selects the frozen capped base-stock family, whose numerical parameters are searched online. Fixed
and stochastic lead times use projected-inventory control and rollouts on common demand and sup-
ply paths, respectively. Runtime uses no language-model calls.
Zero salvage also fixes the rollout boundary condition: inventory left after the last scored period has
no terminal value. The deterministic rule below therefore prices the marginal service benefit of an
order against the holding cost of its projected surplus, without an added continuation credit.
3
SABREAGENT
3.1
DESIGN-TIME ARCHITECTURE
SabreAgent has three independently configurable components: a forecaster (§3.2), an optional
seasonal-shape layer (§3.3), and the policy family searched when lead times are stochastic (§3.5).
We designed the forecaster and the initial policy; DeepSeek-V4-Flash produced the other two arti-
facts before the final configuration was frozen. All language-model calls occur before deployment.
During operation, the policy uses the frozen artifacts to update forecasts and search policy parame-
ters online; a fixed random seed makes these computations reproducible. Restoring all components
to their initial settings gives the frozen core, enabling component ablations within the same policy
implementation (Appendix D).
The two model-authored components use different selection procedures. For policy search, an au-
tomated loop receives the current method, the validation protocol, and the full record of earlier
successes and failures. It proposes one self-contained policy change per round. Candidates advance
according to scores from the validation harness. Candidate scoring uses only generated validation
instances separate from the benchmark test instances. Section 4.1 records the benchmark informa-
tion available during development and the resulting limits on test independence.
Seasonal shapes are frozen per item before benchmark evaluation. The validation instances lack
product text and therefore provide no held-out target for selecting these shapes. The shape layer adds
forecast variants beside the unchanged flat variant; §3.3 states the corresponding log-loss bounds and
their conditions.
4


--- Page 5 ---
Preprint. Work in progress.
3.2
ONLINE FORECASTING IN TWO SPACES
Each instance begins with only five observations, so the forecast bank M uses simple, low-parameter
members and learns their mixture weights online. This choice follows the strong small-sample
performance of simple forecasts and forecast combinations (Makridakis et al., 2020; Hyndman &
Khandakar, 2008). We use discounted Bayesian model averaging (Hoeting et al., 1999; Raftery
et al., 2010), with a forgetting factor γ that discounts past fit geometrically; Appendix D lists the
nine members of one bank and gives the weight update.
For deterministic lead times, nine members are fit in both raw and ϕ(u) = log(1 + u) space, giving
M = 18. The transform can better represent right-skewed weekly demand, while the raw-space
members retain alternative shapes when only five observations are available (Box & Cox, 1964).
The online weights choose between them. Stochastic-lead-time cells use only the raw-space bank
because their decision rule takes a local demand rate as its forecast input.
We compare members across transform spaces through their raw-space scoring densities, using a
change-of-variables correction. A log-space member receives raw-space log density log q(log(1 +
dt)) −log(1 + dt); the Jacobian term is absent for a raw-space member. Omitting it persistently
biases the log-space weights upward relative to the raw-space weights. Lemma 6 quantifies this
bias. For both decision rules, the demand-path sampler uses the learned scoring weights to select
a member; its within-member sampling distribution is specified separately. Member definitions,
scoring densities, and sampling details are in Appendix D.
3.3
PRODUCT TEXT AS A SEASONAL PRIOR
Product descriptions in the real instances provide seasonal timing cues, such as “winter coat”, before
those patterns appear in the short demand history. Synthetic instances lack this text. At design time
we ask DeepSeek-V4-Flash for a 52-week seasonal curve η with mean one, used as a multiplicative
demand factor. We draw three curves per product and aggregate the accepted, normalized samples by
their week-wise median. The aggregate is then clipped, renormalized to mean one, and frozen before
evaluation (Appendix D). The curve encodes relative timing only; the online forecaster continues to
estimate the demand level.
Our validation generator supplies neither product text nor a real calendar for selecting prior strength.
We therefore carry three strengths, α ∈{0, 1/2, 1}. Each runs a copy of the bank on demand
deseasonalized by ηαg, and the variants are weighted online by the same discounted predictive
likelihood used within the bank. The associated Jacobian keeps their raw-space scoring densities
comparable (Appendix D).
The flat variant α = 0 applies no seasonal adjustment and recovers the core forecaster’s scoring
density and path-sampling distribution. Assume uniform initial variant weights and positive mixture
density at every observation. If this variant’s single-period excess log loss relative to the best variant
in that period is always bounded by δ, its mixture weight cannot fall below G−1e−δ/(1−γ), and the
mixture’s per-period excess log loss over it is at most log G + δ/(1 −γ). These discounted bounds
require the stated single-period condition. With undiscounted weights, the cumulative excess log
loss relative to the best fixed variant is at most log G for every sequence; discounting trades that
horizon-free guarantee for adaptation over the year (Proposition 13). Both results characterize the
log loss of the scoring densities; the shape layer’s effect on control reward is evaluated empirically.
3.4
DETERMINISTIC LEAD TIMES
With deterministic L, the order at t first affects available stock at t+L. Theorem 1 characterizes the
zero-lead-time case. Positive lead times introduce a pipeline state (Remark 2), which we handle with
the following projected-inventory surrogate. Write U = dt+L −bIt+L for the shortfall immediately
before that order arrives, where bIt+L is obtained by simulating the committed pipeline. The q-th unit
earns p if U ≥q. Otherwise it contributes to a surplus of (q −U)+ units. Approximating clearance
at predictive mean rate µ, we assign marginal value
m(q) = p P(U ≥q) −h E

The marginal value m(q) defines the surrogate objective
R q
0 m(u) du. The fitted multiplier κ adjusts
the mean-rate clearance approximation. Under the conditions of Proposition 7, m is non-increasing
and q0 = inf{q ≥0 : m(q) ≤0} is the least maximizer of this integrated surrogate. When
κ = 0, this reduces to the nonnegative ρ-fractile of U. The zero-lead-time theorem motivates the
cost-based construction; the implemented deterministic policy uses the fitted depletion multiplier,
including κ = 1 at L = 0. Appendix D.4 gives its parameterization, validation fit, and root search;
§4.1 describes how its functional form was chosen.
The lost-sales recursion projects stock using sales along each sampled path. A textbook inventory-
position target uses cumulative demand over the protection interval (Zipkin, 2000). It therefore treats
demand observed at an empty shelf as if it had reduced inventory position, even though that demand
was lost. For the same sampled path, the textbook shortfall equals our projected shortfall plus the
lost sales inside the interval (Proposition 8). It is thus no smaller on any path, and the means differ
by expected lost sales. This identity concerns shortfalls and their means. The order gap depends on
the nonlinear quantile or crossing in (3). Appendix 3 gives the associated quantile bound.
3.5
STOCHASTIC LEAD TIMES
In the stochastic cells, Lt ∈{1, 2, 3, ∞} and an infinite lead time destroys the order. The re-
alized sequences destroy 32% of synthetic orders and 30% of real orders.
The deterministic
rule in §3.4 assigns an order to one arrival period; stochastic arrivals couple it to several possi-
ble future periods. We evaluate replenishment rules through rollouts over these supply outcomes.
The evaluator’s accounting information identifies whether a positive order survived. Specifically,
qt1{Lt < ∞} = Xt+1 −Xt +At; the survival indicator is therefore known one period later (Propo-
sition 9). We use these observations to update the survival probability used in rollouts.
The policy evaluates a small family of complete replenishment rules over the remaining horizon.
Candidate rules use common simulated demand and supply paths, sharing demand, survival, and
finite-lead-time draws to reduce comparison variance. A coarse pass locates promising parameters,
a local grid refines them jointly, and candidate actions are blended according to estimated value
relative to simulation uncertainty. The full search is specified in Appendix D.
The design-time loop selected the capped base-stock family
K :
q = min
n
(θr −IP)+ , cr
o
,
(4)
where r is a local demand forecast and θ, c are searched online. The position term reacts to low
inventory, while the cap prevents a destroyed order from triggering an arbitrarily large catch-up
order. A pure rate rule sets orders from the demand rate alone, limiting catch-up bursts while leaving
its order unchanged across inventory levels. The capped family contains the pure position family at
c = θ and approaches the pure rate family as θ →∞(Proposition 11). On a finite lost-sales instance
with order destruction, Appendix C provides a numerical certificate of strict reward separation,
conditional on the validity of the estimated slope bounds.
Capped base-stock control is a standard family also used by InventoryBench’s OR baseline. In our
implementation, its cap scales with a local forecast rate, both parameters are selected online for each
instance, and the family was retained by the design-time validation loop. In the small exhaustive
examples in Appendix C, the advantage disappears when the lead-time support prevents surviving
orders from arriving in a lump, and is positive in most nearby configurations where such a lump can
occur.
4
EXPERIMENTS

Figure 3: Performance relative to two hindsight diagnostics. (a) Public baselines against a constant
order-up-to level chosen per instance (dashed) and a clairvoyant supply-feasible upper bound (solid,

cell from the released instance-level results; their weighted means reproduce the published overall
scores. SabreAgent scores 0.6311 against 0.5380 for the best public baseline and leads all six cells.
This comparison varies both model choice and placement: SabreAgent uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash
at design time. The same-model online-adjustment control below measures the effect of adding
bounded per-period adjustments by that model to the complete SabreAgent policy.
Automated selection uses fresh-seed instances generated from the documented synthetic families
and only the five initial demands available to a policy. The harness cannot access benchmark in-
stances, and the final configuration is chosen from validation scores (Appendix F). Reusing this
validation set across rounds incurs adaptive-selection bias within the validation process (Dwork
et al., 2015; Blum & Hardt, 2015). Development also includes two indirect test-informed choices.
We chose the functional form of κ after observing a systematic cell-level mismatch, then fit its co-
efficients on validation. The proposer context contains four aggregate test diagnostics that identify
stochastic supply as the weak regime, although it contains no test score for any proposed candidate.
The reported test result therefore reflects validation-based candidate selection within a development
process informed by these two test-diagnostic channels.

0.0006; values in this figure should therefore be compared within this execution path. Table 1 reports
the official path. The plot decomposes the overall gain, including interaction; the table reports the
frozen core in absolute terms and all other rows as deltas from it.
feasible arrival times and order destruction. Because orders are free and uncapacitated, each unit of
demand can be assigned independently to its latest feasible arrival whenever its profit exceeds the
intervening holding cost (Appendix F). The resulting ex-post upper bound is 0.8656 overall, exactly
1 in both zero-lead-time cells, and 0.6801 and 0.7039 in the stochastic cells. Much of their gap to 1
is therefore imposed by the supply constraints.
With κ = 1 and realized future demand supplied as a point-mass forecast, the projected base-stock
rule matches this bound in all four deterministic cells. This observation concerns the fixed rule
with exact demand inputs; positive-lead-time optimality under a demand distribution is a separate
question. Appendix F specifies the oracle configuration.
A second diagnostic chooses one constant order-up-to level per instance with hindsight and never
revises it. It scores 0.5892, above all ten public baselines overall. The contrast is strongest at lead
time four: the constant scores 0.6220 and 0.4185 on synthetic and real data, compared with 0.5576
and 0.3085 for the strongest public baseline in each cell. At zero lead time, eight of ten baselines
exceed the constant in each cell, so this observation is specific to settings with a protection interval.
4.3
COMPONENT CONTRIBUTIONS AND ONLINE-ADJUSTMENT CONTROL
The frozen OR core reaches 0.6180 on the batched ablation path, above every published baseline’s
overall score. The two model-authored components add +0.0138 on that same path, which is 15%
of the gap between the final score and the strongest public baseline. The seasonal layer acts only on
the three real-data cells, where its paired mean effect is +0.0179. The search layer acts only on the
two stochastic-lead-time cells, where its paired mean effect is +0.0230 (Table 9). Averaging in the
zero effects from the remaining cells reduces their overall deltas. The additive decomposition uses
the batched path throughout; official one-instance-at-a-time scores are reported separately.
Figure 4 crosses three binary choices: seasonal shapes on or off, the initial or selected stochastic
policy family, and the core forecaster or the best alternative found during development. The search
contrast includes both research passes: local-rate normalization from the first and the cap from the
second. Table 8 separates them on validation. This factorial interpretation is valid because accepted
changes affect separate components; Appendix D.7 describes the checks used when composing
them.

Table 2: Same-model online-adjustment control. DeepSeek-V4-Flash adds per-period order ad-

The seasonal and search layers overlap only in the real stochastic cell; their interaction contributes
-0.0016 to the overall weighted mean. The search family and alternative forecaster were selected
from validation candidates. Their test contrasts also reflect the test-informed development choices
described in §4.1. The seasonal shapes were not selected from test outcomes. Paired bootstrap
intervals exclude zero for the seasonal layer, the search layer, and their combination, both overall and
within the cells where each operates. The interval for the pooled forecaster includes zero (Table 9).
For each bootstrap replicate, we sample test instances with replacement and retain the complete
row of scores for all arms, preserving their pairing. Across the 1,320 test instances, the combined
layers yield a single-seed paired mean gain of +0.0139 over the frozen core, with a 95% percentile
interval of [+0.0115, +0.0164] (Table 9). The combined layers change scores on 62% of instances,
with the ten largest movers contributing 14% of total absolute movement. This estimate uses the
instance-level scores for one seed; the +0.0138 gain in Figure 4 averages three seeds. The final con-
figuration’s across-seed standard deviation of 0.0001 measures rollout Monte Carlo noise on fixed
data. Together, these summaries distinguish rollout variability from sensitivity to the composition
of the fixed test set, which is the scope of the paired intervals.
Most proposed changes are rejected. Across two research passes, one of fifty-two candidates con-
tributes to the final search component, and that candidate includes the useful part of the first pass.
No proposal targeting deterministic cells survives validation (Appendix F). This screening record
shows which proposed changes met the validation criterion before deployment.
On the stratified subset in Table 2, we add bounded per-period order adjustments by DeepSeek-
V4-Flash to the complete SabreAgent policy. All four deterministic-cell estimates are negative, but
only the real lead-time-four estimate exceeds two standard errors in magnitude. The two stochastic
estimates are positive. Within this subset, the real stochastic cell is the only cell with a positive
estimate exceeding two standard errors. These results apply to DeepSeek-V4-Flash, this bounded
adjustment rule, and this test subset. Broader conclusions about deterministic supply require further
evaluation.
The highest-scoring validation configuration pools information across instances, which violates the
official one-policy-per-instance protocol. We therefore do not submit it. Its mean gain is +0.0010
over three seeds, while the single-seed paired interval includes zero (Table 9). The submitted con-
figuration preserves the required per-instance information boundary.
Budget and reproducibility.
Producing the shipped artifacts used 674 calls to DeepSeek-V4-
Flash, mostly three shape samples for each of the 200 real products. Calling a model once per
period over the full test set would require 64,200 calls, about 95 times as many (Figure 6). During
operation, a fixed seed makes the policy reproducible; it is rerun end to end and scored with the
official evaluator as detailed in Appendix F.
5
CONCLUSION
On InventoryBench, most of SabreAgent’s performance gain comes from an OR policy that uses the
benchmark’s free replenishment, zero salvage, observable demand, and explicit order destruction.
Product-specific seasonal priors supply timing cues in the real-data cells, and validation selects
a capped base-stock family for lossy supply. These components provide additional gains while
statistical forecasting and inventory optimization determine orders during operation. The final policy
leads every benchmark cell with zero runtime language-model calls.
9


--- Page 10 ---
Preprint. Work in progress.
The zero-lead-time theorem identifies conditions for exact myopic optimality; positive purchase or
setup costs change the value of carried inventory. The controller for positive deterministic lead
times uses a surrogate objective, and the seasonal construction gives predictive-log-loss bounds un-
der the conditions in §3.3. Inventory reward is measured in the benchmark experiments. The online-
adjustment control evaluates bounded order changes by one model on 124 instances. Matched com-
parisons across models and larger samples would clarify when these additional runtime adjustments
improve the complete policy.

A
RELATED WORK
Lost-sales inventory control.
Positive-lead-time lost-sales systems generally require the full
pipeline state, and ordinary base-stock policies need not be optimal (Karlin, 1958; Zipkin, 2008b;a;
Bijvank & Vis, 2011). Different asymptotic regimes favor order-up-to policies when lost-sales penal-
ties grow (Huh et al., 2009), constant-order policies when lead times grow (Goldberg et al., 2016;
Xin & Goldberg, 2016), and capped base-stock policies between those extremes (Xin, 2021). Inven-
toryBench already uses a capped base-stock baseline (Baek et al., 2026). Building on this established
family, we connect the cap to catch-up bursts caused by destroyed orders, scale it by a local demand
rate, and select both parameters online. Theorem 1 concerns a different, degenerate regime: without
purchase or setup costs there is no speculative or batching motive, and instantaneous replenishment
removes protection-time value as well.
Data-driven inventory policies and forecasting.
Data-driven approaches replace a known dis-
tribution with samples (Levi et al., 2007), estimate decisions from features (Ban & Rudin, 2019),
or train policies on simulated and operational data (Gijsbrechts et al., 2022; Oroojlooyjadid et al.,
2022; Qi et al., 2023). InventoryBench instead provides five initial observations and no cross-series
training set, which favors a mixture of simple models over a flexible learned forecaster. Discounted
predictive-likelihood weighting is standard (Hoeting et al., 1999; Raftery et al., 2010), as are the
short-sample forecasting members we combine (Makridakis et al., 2020; Hyndman & Khandakar,
2008). The technical detail specific to our mixture is that members fit in different transform spaces
must be scored as densities of the same raw observation; otherwise the omitted Jacobian systemati-
cally favors the log-space members.
Language models for search and decision making.
Verifier-guided systems use a language
model to propose an artifact and an external evaluator to retain or reject it (Romera-Paredes et al.,
2024; Liu et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026). The closest pattern
is language-model variation inside evolutionary search over heuristics (Hemberg et al., 2024). In
operations research, prior work has translated natural language into formal models checked by a
solver (Ramamonjison et al., 2023; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2024). SabreAgent ap-
plies this established search pattern to policy-family design. This choice also reflects evidence that
language models remain unreliable as planners or self-correctors (Valmeekam et al., 2023; Huang
et al., 2024; Kambhampati et al., 2024) and can show systematic biases in newsvendor decisions
(Liu et al., 2025).
13


--- Page 14 ---
Preprint. Work in progress.
Text-derived priors for cold starts.
Language models have also been adapted for time-series
forecasting (Gruver et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), although some reported gains
survive removal of the language component (Tan et al., 2024). Our seasonal layer uses product
descriptions to elicit a prior over relative demand timing. Related work has used language models to
infer priors from metadata, mix parametric priors over prompts, or produce predictive beliefs from
textual descriptions (Garthwaite et al., 2005; Choi et al., 2022; Capstick et al., 2025; Requeima et al.,
2024; Selby et al., 2025). The resulting seasonal variant always competes with a statistical variant
without seasonal adjustment. This design addresses the benchmark’s cold start. When retailer data
on comparable products are available, clustering, attribute regression, and life-cycle models provide
more directly grounded signals (Thomassey & Fiordaliso, 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2019;
Van Steenbergen & Mes, 2020; Fildes et al., 2022).
B
PROOFS
Theorem 1 is the one result the main text states formally, and it is restated here before it is proved,
so the restatement carries a fresh number. The six results after it are discussed there in prose and
stated formally only here, one to a subsection, in the order the main text raises them. Standing
conventions: demand is nonnegative and integrable, p > 0 and h > 0, ρ = p/(p + h) ∈(0, 1), and
(x)+ = max{x, 0}. For a random variable Z we write FZ(z) = P(Z ≤z) and FZ(z−) = P(Z <
z), which differ exactly at the atoms of Z; this distinction determines the one-sided conditions in
Proposition 7 and is kept throughout.
Two distinctions organize the results. The exact-optimality clause of Theorem 1 rests on Assump-
tion 2; §B.1 states this condition and gives a counterexample when it fails. Proposition 8 gives an
exact identity for shortfalls and their means, together with bounds for the corresponding quantile
gaps (§B.4).
B.1
THEOREM 1: ZERO OPTION VALUE AT L = 0
Assumption 1 (the zero-option setting, restated from §2.2). The per-period reward is p st −h Iend

known marginals Ft.

Lemma 2 is where the zero purchase cost enters. A unit purchase cost cb > 0 would replace the
objective in (5) by Jt(y) −cb(y −It), in which the entering inventory appears as a linear credit, not
only through the constraint y ≥It; a carried unit would then save cb at every later period, which is
precisely the option value the theorem denies.
For the exact-optimality clause of Theorem 1, we state the non-decreasing-fractile condition as a
separate assumption.

below show that it cannot be dropped.

whenever It ≤y∗
t , and the myopic newsvendor solution is exactly optimal, not asymptotically or
approximately so.
This restatement is the conditional half of Theorem 1. The unconditional half, that Vt is non-
increasing and that no post-order level above max{I, y∗
t } is strictly better, needs neither Assump-
tion 2 nor the induction below and is separated out as Proposition 5. It is the half the design of §3.4
rests on, so the two are proved apart to keep visible which one carries which hypothesis.
The benchmark fixes each instance’s demand path in advance and takes the expectation over the
policy’s own randomization alone (§2.1), while the theorem treats demand as random with known
marginals Ft. The theorem describes the policy’s stochastic planning model. Taking Ft = δdt
degenerate recovers the latter, and the myopic policy then becomes the clairvoyant rule that §4.2
measures.
Proof. Backward induction on t, with induction hypothesis the conjunction
(H1) Vt+1 is constant on [0, y∗
t+1], and (H2) Vt+1 is non-increasing on [0, ∞),
where for t + 1 = T + 1 we read y∗
T +1 = +∞.
Base case. At t = T the continuation is VT +1 ≡0, which is constant on all of [0, ∞) and non-
increasing, so (H1) and (H2) hold. This is the only place the zero salvage value is used, and it is
used decisively: a salvage credit ς > 0 would give VT +1(I) = ς I, which is strictly increasing and
violates both halves of the hypothesis at once.
Inductive step. Assume (H1) and (H2) at t + 1 and fix t ≤T.
Step 1: the continuation is non-increasing. For every d ≥0 the map y 7→(y −d)+ is non-
decreasing, so by (H2) the map y 7→Vt+1((y −d)+) is non-increasing; taking expectations, Ct is
non-increasing on [0, ∞). Independence of dt from the past is what makes Ct a function of y alone.
Step 2, the key step: the continuation is flat below the myopic level. Let 0 ≤y ≤y∗
t . Then
(y −d)+ ≤y ≤y∗
t ≤y∗
t+1 for every d ≥0, where the last inequality is Assumption 2. So the
15


--- Page 16 ---
Preprint. Work in progress.
argument of Vt+1 lies in [0, y∗
t+1] pathwise, and (H1) gives Vt+1((y −dt)+) = Vt+1(0) almost
surely. Hence Ct(y) = Vt+1(0) for all y ∈[0, y∗
t ]: on that range the continuation contributes an
additive constant, and the first-order condition for Jt is the first-order condition for Gt alone. This
is the mechanism the theorem asserts. It is available because ordering is free and instantaneous, so
any unit not carried forward can be replaced at t + 1 at no cost, which is exactly what makes Vt+1
flat below its own target.
Step 3: y∗
t maximizes Jt. On [0, y∗
t ] we have Jt = Gt + Vt+1(0), which by Lemma 2 is non-
decreasing and is maximized over that interval at y∗
t . For y > y∗
t , Lemma 2 gives Gt(y) ≤Gt(y∗
t )
and Step 1 gives Ct(y) ≤Ct(y∗
t ), so Jt(y) ≤Jt(y∗
t ). Therefore y∗
t maximizes Jt over [0, ∞), and
Jt is non-increasing on [y∗
t , ∞) because both of its terms are.
Step 4: re-establishing the hypothesis at t. For I ≤y∗
t the unconstrained maximizer y∗
t is feasible,
so Vt(I) = Jt(y∗
t ). For I > y∗
t the objective is non-increasing on the feasible set [I, ∞) by
Step 3, so the supremum is attained at y = I and Vt(I) = Jt(I). Both cases are summarized
by Vt(I) = Jt(max{I, y∗
t }), which is the claimed optimal post-order level. It follows that Vt is
constant on [0, y∗
t ], giving (H1) at t, and that Vt is non-increasing on [0, ∞), since it is constant up
to y∗
t and equals Jt, which is non-increasing, above it. This gives (H2) at t and closes the induction.
Zero marginal value of carried stock is (H1) read as a difference: for 0 ≤I′ ≤I ≤y∗
t , Vt(I) −
Vt(I′) = 0. Optimality of yt = max{It, y∗
t } is Step 4 applied at every period. That a Markov
policy attaining the per-period maximum in (5) is optimal among all history-dependent policies
is the verification theorem for a finite-horizon problem with bounded-below rewards and a one-
dimensional Borel state (Bertsekas & Shreve, 1978); the expectation E[Vt+1((y −dt)+)] is defined
because Vt+1 is monotone and hence Borel.
Zero fixed ordering cost is also part of the theorem’s setting. With a setup charge K > 0 the period
objective becomes Jt(y) −K1{y > I}, which is not concave in y, so Lemma 2 no longer identifies
the maximizer and the optimal policy is of (s, S) form, no longer base-stock (Scarf, 1960). Under
K > 0 it is optimal not to order at all for entering inventories somewhat below the target, so Vt is
not flat on [0, y∗
t ] and the conclusion fails even though the mechanism of Step 2 is untouched.
The effect of decreasing myopic levels depends on the reachable leftover inventory. A high-demand
period preceding a low one is not by itself enough to break exact optimality. Because ordering is free,
Vt+1 is flat on [0, y∗
t+1] by (H1), so carrying surplus into t + 1 costs nothing while the leftover stays
under the next level, the policy having been going to order up to it in any case. What breaking exact
optimality needs is that the drop be reachable, P((y∗
t −dt)+ > y∗
t+1) > 0: only then does a unit
ordered at the fractile face a period in which no order would have been placed for it. Reachability is
necessary and not sufficient, since the holding it exposes the unit to must also outweigh the current
period’s marginal value. Exact backward induction over a bounded integer state exhibits all three
cases. With y∗falling from 17 to 11 but demand never below 12, so that the leftover cannot exceed
11, the myopic level stays optimal at every state despite the drop; with a reach probability of 0.012
it is still optimal; and with y∗falling from 16 to 1 at a reach probability of 0.714 the optimum drops
six units below the fractile.
Corollary 4 (integer orders). Assume in addition that dt is integer valued and that the post-order
level is restricted to the integers, as the benchmark’s flooring of order quantities enforces. Then
Gt(y + 1) −Gt(y) = p −(p + h)Ft(y) for integer y, this difference is non-increasing in y, and
the smallest integer y with Ft(y) ≥ρ maximizes Gt over the integers. Under the hypotheses of
Theorem 3 the optimal integer post-order level is max{It, y∗,Z
t
}, where y∗,Z
t
= min{k ∈Z :
Ft(k) ≥ρ}.
Proof. For integer valued d and integer y, min(d, y + 1) −min(d, y) = 1{d ≥y + 1} and
(y + 1 −d)+ −(y −d)+ = 1{d ≤y}. Taking expectations, Gt(y + 1) −Gt(y) = p P(dt >
y)−h P(dt ≤y) = p−(p+h)Ft(y), which is non-increasing in y because Ft is non-decreasing. A
function on Z with non-increasing forward differences is maximized at the first y where the forward
difference turns non-positive, that is at the smallest integer with Ft(y) ≥ρ.
Such an integer is a ρ-fractile of Ft, but Assumption 2 is a property of a selection and the integer
selection need not inherit it: with d1 uniform on {2, 5} and d2 uniform on {1, 4} at ρ = 1/2,
the monotone selection (2, 2) exists while y∗,Z = (2, 1) decreases. The theorem therefore cannot

The next result gives the upper-bound property under the zero-option setting alone; the following
example identifies the role of Assumption 2 in exact optimality.
Proposition 5 (what survives without monotone myopic levels). Let Assumption 1 hold with inde-
pendent, integrable demands, and let y∗
t be any ρ-fractile of Ft. Then for every t and every I ≥0,
Vt(I) =
sup

Jt(y),
(6)
and Vt is non-increasing on [0, ∞). In words, ordering above the myopic fractile never strictly pays,
so some optimal post-order level lies at or below max{I, y∗
t }: the myopic level bounds the optimum
from above and never from below. When the fractile is not unique a higher level can tie, which is
why the statement is (6) and not a claim that every optimal level is at or below it.
Proof. That Vt is non-increasing is immediate from (5), since the feasible sets {y ≥I} shrink as
I grows, and it needs no induction. Given this at t + 1, Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 3 applies
verbatim and Ct is non-increasing; with Lemma 2 this makes Jt non-increasing on [y∗
t , ∞), so no
y > max{I, y∗
t } can improve on max{I, y∗
t }, which is (6).
Remark 1. Assumption 2 is used only in Step 2, and only to guarantee that the reachable states
(y −d)+ for y ≤y∗
t stay inside the flat region [0, y∗
t+1] of Vt+1. When the myopic levels decrease
over time this can fail, and where it does it fails in a direction: stock left over from t can land
above the next period’s target, where it is charged holding without displacing any future order, so
the true optimum orders strictly less than the myopic fractile. A decrease is not by itself enough,
since Step 2 needs only (y∗
t −essinf dt)+ ≤y∗
t+1, which is strictly weaker than Assumption 2 and
can hold while the levels fall; the discussion after Theorem 3 exhibits both sides numerically. The
failure direction is the same as the inequality of Proposition 5. The depletion term κ of Proposition 7
acts in the same direction; κ remains an empirical correction fitted for a separate effect.
Example 1 (the hypothesis cannot be dropped). Take T = 2, p = h = 1 so ρ = 1/2, demands
independent with d1 ∼Uniform[0, 100] and d2 ≡0. Every hypothesis of Assumption 1 holds, and
y∗
1 = 50 while y∗
2 = 0, so Assumption 2 fails. In period 2 the reward of a post-order level y ≥I is
−y, so V2(I) = −I. Hence
J1(y) = E[min(d1, y)] −E (y −d1)+ −E (y −d1)+ = E[min(d1, y)] −2 E (y −d1)+ ,
and for y ∈[0, 100] this is y −3y2/200, maximized at y = 100/3 with value 50/3 ≈16.67,
whereas the myopic level y∗
1 = 50 yields 12.5. The myopic policy is strictly suboptimal, and
V1(I) = J1(max{I, 100/3}) is strictly decreasing on (100/3, 50], so V1 is not constant on [0, y∗
1]
either. Both halves of the conclusion of Theorem 3 fail, while (6) holds with room to spare.
Remark 2 (the pipeline state at L > 0). The zero-lead-time assumption is essential to Theorem 3.
At L > 0, the order placed at t lands at t + L, so the inventory it creates cannot be topped up
before it arrives and the states reachable at t + 1, . . . , t + L depend on y through the entire pipeline
vector rather than a scalar. Step 2 is the step that fails: the continuation is no longer flat in the
current decision, because a shortage inside the protection interval cannot be repaired by a free order
that arrives in time, so carried stock does acquire option value and the one-dimensional dynamic
program (5) is not the right object. Lost-sales systems with positive lead time have no known simple
optimal policy and a state that is the whole pipeline (Zipkin, 2008a;b; Bijvank & Vis, 2011). The rule
of §3.4 uses Theorem 3 as a design motivation for a surrogate objective. It assigns surplus beyond
the responsibility period holding costs without a continuation credit, and prices the responsibility
period through the explicit marginal condition of Proposition 7. The proposition characterizes the
maximizers of the integrated surrogate; dynamic optimality remains specific to the zero-lead-time
setting.

Preprint. Work in progress.
B.2
LEMMA 6: COMPARABILITY OF TWO TRANSFORM SPACES
Lemma 6 (Two-space comparability). Let γ ∈(0, 1), let ϕ be strictly increasing and differen-
tiable with ϕ′ > 0, and let a member be fitted on z = ϕ(d) with predictive density q. Then
the member’s predictive density in raw space is q(ϕ(d)) ϕ′(d), so its raw-space predictive log-
density is log q(ϕ(d)) + log ϕ′(d). For ϕ(d) = log(1 + d) on d ≥0 the correction is log ϕ′(d) =
−log(1 + d) ≤0. Suppose this correction is omitted. Then the log-weight of every log-space mem-
ber is inflated by log(1 + dt) per period relative to every identity-space member, whose correction
is zero, and under the discounted update ℓt = γℓt−1 + (log-density) the induced relative offset ∆t
obeys ∆t = γ∆t−1 + log(1 + dt) with ∆0 = 0, so
E∆t = 1 −γt
1 −γ E[log(1 + d)] −−−→
t→∞
E[log(1 + d)]
1 −γ
for identically distributed integrable log(1 + dt). The offset does not cancel in the softmax and does
not vanish as data accumulate.
Proof. Change of variables. Since ϕ is strictly increasing, {Y ≤d} = {Z ≤ϕ(d)} for Z = ϕ(Y ),
so the raw-space distribution function is FY (d) = Q(ϕ(d)) with Q the distribution function of Z.
Differentiating and using differentiability of ϕ gives the density fY (d) = q(ϕ(d))ϕ′(d), and taking
logarithms gives the stated decomposition. For ϕ(d) = log(1 + d) we have ϕ′(d) = 1/(1 + d) and
log ϕ′(d) = −log(1 + d), which is nonpositive for d ≥0 and zero only at d = 0.
Accumulation. Write ℓc
t,m for the log-weight accumulated with the correction and ℓo
t,m for the one
that omits it. Both obey the same recursion with per-period increments differing by −log ϕ′
m(dt),
so ∆t,m = ℓo
t,m −ℓc
t,m satisfies ∆t,m = γ∆t−1,m −log ϕ′
m(dt) with ∆0,m = 0. For an identity-
space member log ϕ′
m ≡0 and ∆t,m ≡0; for a log1p member the increment is log(1 + dt) ≥0.
First consider the deterministic recursion lt = γlt−1 + b with a constant offset b and γ ∈(0, 1):
subtracting the fixed point b/(1−γ) gives lt−b/(1−γ) = γ(lt−1−b/(1−γ)), hence lt = γtl0+b(1−
γt)/(1 −γ) →b/(1 −γ) geometrically. Taking expectations in the stochastic recursion and using
that E[log(1 + dt)] = b does not depend on t puts E∆t,m in exactly this form with l0 = 0, which is
the displayed limit. When the demands are in addition independent, ∆t,m = P
s<t γs log(1+dt−s)
converges in distribution to P
s≥0 γs log(1 + d−s), a proper random variable with mean b/(1 −γ);
the deterministic statement is the statement about its mean.
Non-cancellation. The softmax is invariant under a shift common to all members: for any c ∈R,
exp(ℓm+c)/ P
m′ exp(ℓm′+c) = exp(ℓm)/ P
m′ exp(ℓm′). A Jacobian correction identical across
members would therefore be immaterial, and this is why one can omit a shared normalizing constant
with no consequence. The correction here is not shared: it is 0 on the nine identity-space members
and −log(1+dt) on the nine log1p members. What survives in the weights is the difference, and for
a log1p member m and an identity member m′ the omitted version multiplies the odds wt,m/wt,m′
by exp(∆t,m), whose logarithm has expectation tending to E[log(1 + d)]/(1 −γ). Since d ≥0
the offset has a fixed sign, so it is a standing tilt, not a fluctuation that averages out, and because
the limit is a nonzero constant whenever P(d > 0) > 0 it does not shrink as the series lengthens.
Adding log ϕ′ is thus sufficient to put the two halves of the bank on one scale, and it is necessary up
to a member-independent additive constant, since those are exactly the transformations the softmax
cannot see.
At the shipped γ = 0.92 the geometric sum is 1/(1−γ) = 12.5 periods, so a series running at a level
of about one hundred units, where log(1+d) ≈4.6, produces a steady-state log-odds tilt of roughly
58 nats in favor of the log1p half of the bank. At this scale, omitting the correction concentrates the
mixture weight on the log1p space.

which is linear convergence. The initial bracket used by the numerical procedure is valid: it takes

orders to the nonnegative domain and using the infimum definition in (iv) gives q0 = (q)+. At
an atom, the two one-sided inequalities apply; an equality such as P(U < q) = ρ need not hold.
The empirical strict-inequality frequency used to evaluate Φ is consistent with this infimum defini-
tion.
B.4
PROPOSITION 8: PATHWISE OVER-ORDERING UNDER LOST SALES
This proposition derives an accounting identity on each fixed sample path, valid for every demand
distribution. The probabilistic statements then follow from the pathwise equalities.
Set-up.
Fix a period t and a deterministic lead time L ≥0 with t + L ≤T, without which dt+L
does not exist and orders scheduled past the horizon sit in Xt without ever arriving. At the decision
epoch of period t the policy holds It on hand and Xt in transit, and IPt = It + Xt. Because the
lead time is deterministic, an order placed at t −j lands at t −j + L, so the orders still outstanding
at the decision epoch of t are exactly those placed at t −L, . . . , t −1 and they land in periods
t, . . . , t + L −1; the order placed at t lands at t + L, and every later order lands after t + L. Let
Aj be arrivals in period j, sj = min(dj, Ij + Aj) the units sold and λj = (dj −(Ij + Aj))+ the
demand lost, so that sj = dj −λj by definition of the minimum. Write Λ = Pt+L−1
j=t
λj for the
lost sales realized inside the protection interval, and let bIt+L = It+L be the on-hand stock at the
decision epoch of t + L, that is, before the order placed at t lands.
Proposition 8 (Lost-sales over-ordering of the textbook rule). With the notation above, put U naive =
Pt+L
j=t dj −IPt and U proj = dt+L −bIt+L. Then
U naive = U proj + Λ
pathwise.
(8)
Consequently U naive ≥U proj pathwise, hence U naive dominates U proj stochastically; T(U naive) ≥
T(U proj) for every functional T with the monotonicity property that T(U + Λ) ≥T(U) whenever
Λ ≥0 almost surely, a class that contains every quantile and the mean; the two shortfalls agree
almost surely if and only if Λ = 0 almost surely, that is if and only if the shelf never empties inside
the protection interval; EU naive −EU proj = EΛ when both are integrable; and Λ is non-decreasing
in L along a fixed arrival stream.
Proof. The on-hand recursion is Ij+1 = Ij + Aj −sj, which is an identity because holding is

The consequences follow. Since λj ≥0 we have Λ ≥0 pathwise, so U naive ≥U proj pathwise and
P(U naive > x) ≥P(U proj > x) for every x, which is first-order stochastic dominance. If T has
the stated monotonicity then T(U naive) = T(U proj + Λ) ≥T(U proj); the mean has it by linearity
and monotonicity of the integral, and the ρ-quantile has it because U proj ≤U naive pathwise implies
FU naive ≤FU proj pointwise and hence the corresponding generalized inverses are ordered. Equality
almost surely holds if and only if Λ = 0 almost surely, and Λ = 0 if and only if λj = 0 for
every j in the interval, which is exactly the statement that demand is fully served, so the shelf never
empties inside t, . . . , t + L −1. Taking expectations in (8) gives EU naive −EU proj = EΛ. Finally
Λ = Λ(L) = Pt+L−1
j=t
λj is a sum of nonnegative terms, so Λ(L + 1) = Λ(L) + λt+L ≥Λ(L):
the quantity is non-decreasing in the length of the interval along a fixed realized trajectory, that is,
holding the arrivals and the demands fixed and lengthening the window. This monotonicity concerns
the window length on a fixed trajectory as its window length L increases. A change in L in the
closed-loop system also changes the policy, the orders and hence the λj themselves.
Remark 3 (order-quantity gaps and EΛ). Proposition 8 says the naive shortfall exceeds the projected
one by Λ pathwise and by EΛ in mean. The order-quantity gap depends on the quantile or crossing
functional used in §3.4; a gap of EΛ applies to the means. For random variables with U naive =
U proj + Λ and Λ ≥0, all that holds in general is 0 ≤qρ(U naive) −qρ(U proj) ≤esssup Λ. Both
bounds can be attained: with U proj ≡0 and Λ = 2 · Bernoulli(1/2) one has EΛ = 1 while the
medians of the two shortfalls are both 0, so the difference of the targets is 0 while the mean gap is
EΛ. Order quantities retain the unconditional ordering; the gap size depends on the functional.
B.5
PROPOSITION 9: EXACT IDENTIFICATION OF DESTROYED ORDERS
The accounting.
The benchmark’s runner maintains a schedule sched[·] of units due to land in
each future period, and reports to the policy the in-transit total Xt = P
u≥t schedt[u], evaluated
at the decision epoch of t, that is before anything in period t has happened. Within period t the
evaluator performs, in this order: (a) the policy places qt; (b) if Lt < ∞, sched[t+Lt] is incremented
by qt, and if Lt = ∞nothing is scheduled and the order is destroyed; (c) At := sched[t] is delivered
to on-hand stock and sched[t] is set to zero; (d) sales and holding are booked, which do not touch
the schedule. Orders scheduled to land beyond the end of the horizon are never delivered but remain
in the schedule and hence in X.
Proposition 9 (Exact supply identification). Under the accounting above, for every period t,
qt1{Lt < ∞} = Xt+1 −Xt + At.
(9)
Hence whenever qt > 0 the indicator 1{Lt < ∞} is a function of quantities the policy has observed
by the decision epoch of t + 1, and is identified exactly, with no inference. For t = T there is no
such epoch and the last order’s fate is never available to the policy, though the identity itself still
holds. Under an accounting in which an order with Lt = ∞enters the reported in-transit total
and is never removed from it, the same combination equals qt identically and the indicator is not
identified at all.
Proof. Write St(·) for the schedule at the decision epoch of t, so Xt = P
u≥t St[u]. Step (b) adds
qt1{Lt < ∞} to the entry at index t + Lt ≥t, which is in the range of the sum, including the case
21


--- Page 22 ---
Preprint. Work in progress.
Lt = 0 where the index is t itself, and including the case t + Lt > T where the entry is never
delivered but is still counted. Therefore after (b)
X
u≥t
S[u] = Xt + qt1{Lt < ∞} .
Step (c) reads At = S[t] at that moment and then zeroes that entry, which removes exactly At from
the sum and leaves the entries at indices u ≥t+1 untouched. Step (d) does not modify the schedule,
so the schedule at the decision epoch of t + 1 satisfies
Xt+1 =
X
u≥t+1
St+1[u] = Xt + qt1{Lt < ∞} −At,
which rearranges to (9).
For the identification claim, the policy knows qt, which it placed, and observes Xt at the decision
epoch of t and both Xt+1 and At at the decision epoch of t+1, since the previous period’s arrivals are
part of the reported state. So the right-hand side of (9) is measurable with respect to the information
Ht+1 available at that epoch, and when qt > 0 the indicator is recovered as the ratio of the right-
hand side to qt. When qt = 0 the identity reads 0 = 0 and the indicator is not recovered, which is
immaterial: no order was placed, so no trial took place.
The deployed rule tests the ratio against 1
2 instead of against 1. The two tests agree exactly here,
because orders are floored before being placed, so the delivered amount is either the full order or
zero and no intermediate value can arise. The threshold is a guard against a fractional order reaching
the comparison, not a relaxation of the identity.
For the retaining accounting, suppose instead that step (b) adds qt to a pending list regardless of
Lt and that only finite-lead orders are ever removed, on delivery. Then the reported total X′ obeys
X′
t+1 = X′
t + qt −At for every t, so X′
t+1 −X′
t + At = qt identically. The map from the
unobserved indicator to the observed triple (X′
t, X′
t+1, At) is constant in the indicator, so no function
of the observables can distinguish a surviving order from a destroyed one at t + 1, so the parameter
is unidentified, not merely hard to estimate. That accounting also leaves destroyed orders in X′
forever, so a rule of the form q = (S −IP)+ is throttled by stock that will never arrive, its subtrahend
growing with every destroyed order until the rule falls silent.
Corollary 10 (the survival probability is a posterior mean over observed trials). Let T = {t : qt >
0} and Bt = 1{Lt < ∞} for t ∈T . By Proposition 9 each Bt is Ht+1-measurable. Modeling
{Bt}t∈T as independent Bernoulli(π) with a Beta(1, 1) prior on π, the posterior after the trials
completed by period t is Beta(1+nsurv
t
, 1+nord
t
−nsurv
t
) with posterior mean (1+nsurv
t

t
),
where nord
t
counts the completed trials and nsurv
t
the survivals among them.
Proof. Measurability is Proposition 9. The trial set is chosen by the policy, so the factorization
needs one more step: the order is placed before Lt is realized, so {t ∈T } = {qt > 0} is Ht-
measurable and the trials are selected by a predictable rule, under which the likelihood of (Bt)t∈T
still factorizes. Beta-Bernoulli conjugacy then gives the posterior and its mean. The content of the
corollary lies in the observable input: the trials are observed, so the estimator applies conjugacy
directly to the recovered survival data. Under the retaining accounting of Proposition 9 the Bt are
not observable and no such estimator exists.
B.6
PROPOSITION 11: CONTAINMENT AND CONDITIONAL NUMERICAL SEPARATION
Proposition 11 (Containment and conditional numerical separation). Consider decision rules map-
ping a state with local forecast rate r > 0 and inventory position IP ≥0 to an order, and let
B = {q = (θr −IP)+ : θ ≥0},
R = {q = cr : c ≥0},
K = {q = min((θr −IP)+ , cr) : θ ≥0, c ≥0}.
Then B ⊆K exactly, by the choice c = θ. For every fixed state, the capped rule with param-
eters (θ, c) equals the rate rule with parameter c as soon as θ ≥c + IP/r, and in particular
min((θr −IP)+ , cr) →cr as θ →∞. If the inventory positions reachable on an instance are
22


--- Page 23 ---
Preprint. Work in progress.
bounded and the local rate is bounded below by rmin > 0, which holds on any finite-horizon in-
stance with bounded demand and bounded orders, then R ⊆K on that instance for finite θ. In all
cases B ∪R ⊆K, and on every instance with P
t |Rt| integrable
sup
π∈K
E[P
t Rt(π)] ≥
sup
π∈B∪R
E[P
t Rt(π)] .
For a constructed lost-sales instance with P(L = ∞) > 0, the numerical certificate in Appendix C
establishes strict reward separation conditional on the validity of its estimated slope bounds. The
containment claims are proved below; the construction and certificate are described under Numer-
ical separation.
Proof. For the first claim, take c = θ. Since IP ≥0 we have (θr −IP)+ ≤θr = cr, so the
minimum is attained by the first argument and the capped rule reproduces the base-stock rule state
by state, not merely in a limit. For the second, if θr −IP ≥cr, equivalently θ ≥c + IP/r, then
(θr −IP)+ ≥cr and the minimum is cr; for fixed r > 0 and finite IP the left-hand side (θr −IP)+
increases without bound as θ →∞, so the threshold is eventually met and the pointwise limit is cr.
If the reachable positions satisfy IP ≤B < ∞and r ≥rmin > 0, then a single finite θ ≥c+B/rmin
makes the two rules agree at every reachable state, so they generate the same trajectory on every
sample path and the same expected reward. The inequality between suprema then holds term by
term: every member of B is a member of K, and every member of R is either a member of K under
the boundedness condition or a pointwise limit of members of K whose values agree with it for all
large θ. That agreement is pathwise, the threshold θ depending on the path through its bound on IP,
so dominated convergence under the integrability hypothesis carries it from trajectories to expected
rewards.
Corollary 12. On every instance the best member of K is at least as good as the best member of
B ∪R. The family the search of §3.5 ranges over therefore has a best member at least as good as
the first pass’s. This comparison concerns the best members of the families. The shipped search re-
solves each period and returns a softmax-weighted blend of candidate actions, with value differences
scaled by the median standard error; its realized performance is evaluated empirically.
Proof. Immediate from Proposition 11.
Numerical separation.
A constructed instance examines the reward advantage of the larger fam-
ily. The witness is the constructed instance of §C: constant demand 10, horizon 5, p = h = 1, empty
initial inventory, lead times drawn independently and uniformly from {1, 2, 3, ∞} per period, and
the local rate held at the mean demand. The expectation over lead-time sequences is a finite sum
over its 45 = 1024 atoms, each evaluated in closed form, so the expected rewards at the three grid
optima are exact up to floating-point arithmetic, and the capped grid optimum strictly beats both
pure grid optima. Appendix C gives the construction, the enumeration method and the numbers for
six configurations, and bounds the two pure families from above on the witness instance to account
for grid resolution. Those bounds use slopes measured on a grid. Strict reward separation there-
fore has a numerical certificate for this construction, conditional on the validity of the slope bounds
estimated on the grid.
The mechanism.
The construction isolates three ingredients of the arrival-lumping mechanism
relevant to the benchmark. Orders are destroyed with positive probability, so a rule that reads the
inventory position sees a gap open that no arrival will close. A pure base-stock member responds by
re-ordering the entire gap, because that is all the rule can do: its action is a function of the position
error alone. When that catch-up order and its successor both survive and their lead times differ by
exactly the gap between their placement dates, they land in the same period, and the shelf receives
in one period what was meant to cover several. Holding is charged on ending inventory every period
until the lump burns off at the demand rate, and at ρ = 0.5 one extra period of holding cancels a
unit’s entire margin, so the lump is expensive in proportion to its size. A pure rate member bounds
each period’s order by cr independently of inventory position, avoiding position-driven catch-up
bursts while continuing to order after a lump arrives for another reason. The capped base-stock rule
is the smallest family we know of with both properties, since it is a function of the position gap and
of the rate at once and its action is the smaller of the two, so it tracks the level while refusing to
place a catch-up lump.
23


--- Page 24 ---
Preprint. Work in progress.
The control configuration isolates the effect of lead-time support. Restrict the lead-time support to
{1, ∞} and no two surviving orders can ever land together, so the lumping mechanism is unavailable
by construction; the separation gap there is exactly zero. Where two distinct finite lead times are
available the gap opens in four of the five configurations tested and closes in the fifth, at ρ = 0.95
with T = 5, where holding is cheap enough that suppressing the catch-up lump costs more than it
saves. One further period restores it, so that closure belongs to the horizon at the same ρ. These
controlled comparisons support the mechanism within the tested configurations.
B.7
PROPOSITION 13: LOG-LOSS BOUNDS FOR THE SHAPE LAYER
Set-up.
Index the shape variants by g ∈{1, . . . , G}, so that every sum over g below has exactly

Remark 4 (adaptation and per-period guarantees under discounting). Part (ii) is a per-period bound
and summing it over the horizon yields T(log G+δ/(1−γ)), which grows linearly in T. Discounting
reduces the influence of older observations so that variants can gain weight as their fit improves.
Alternating which variant fits best can incur a switching cost every period, so excess over a fixed
comparator can grow with the horizon. For γ < 1, the result established here is the conditional
per-period bound and the accompanying weight floor, which keeps the flat variant available after a
run of bad periods.
Remark 5 (scoring-density equivalence and sample-path reproducibility). The flat variant repro-
duces the core forecaster’s scoring density exactly, as required by Proposition 13. Its random draws
follow a separate sampling stream: selecting a variant consumes randomness before the bank is
sampled, and each variant runs a private copy of the bank with its own seed, so even when the flat
variant carries essentially all of the weight the realized sample paths differ from those of the unlay-
ered forecaster. Bit-identity holds only where the layer is absent entirely, which is the case on the
synthetic instances: they carry no product description, no shape is requested, the shape axis is never
instantiated, and the forecaster object is left untouched. Bit-identity in this case follows directly
from the construction.
C
NUMERICAL VERIFICATION OF PROPOSITION 11
Proposition 11 establishes containment, B ∪R ⊆K, with B ⊆K exactly. The finite-horizon
instance below examines strict reward separation through exhaustive enumeration and a numerical
certificate conditional on the validity of estimated slope bounds. Every reported value describes this
construction; benchmark performance is evaluated in the experiments.
25


--- Page 26 ---
Preprint. Work in progress.
C.1
THE INSTANCE
A single product at a single location, starting empty, over a horizon of T periods. Demand is constant
at 10 units per period, so the three families use the same known demand rate: the local rate r used
by all families is fixed at the mean demand, r = 10, in every period and for every candidate. The
unit profit and unit holding cost are stated per configuration below. The lead time Lt is drawn
independently in each period from a stated support that includes ∞, uniformly over the support; a
draw of ∞destroys the order, which never arrives and never enters the in-transit total.
The period runs in the benchmark’s order: the policy places its order; if the lead time is finite the
order is scheduled to land at t + Lt; arrivals scheduled for t are added to on-hand stock; demand is
served from stock and unmet demand is lost; holding is charged on the ending inventory. An order
scheduled beyond the end of the horizon is never delivered. The three families are exactly the pure
base-stock, pure rate and capped base-stock families of §3.5, with the pure limits realized by setting
the inactive parameter to 106. Orders are real-valued here, so all three families are evaluated as
continua under the same convention, with integer rounding disabled.
C.2
HOW THE EXPECTATION IS COMPUTED
The expectation is over the lead-time sequence alone, and the horizon is short enough that this
expectation is a finite sum. With a support of size S and horizon T there are ST sequences; we
enumerate all of them, weight each by its probability, and evaluate the resulting trajectory in closed
form. The reported values and their differences are finite sums, exact up to floating-point arithmetic
and free of Monte Carlo error.
Each family’s optimum is taken over a grid of step 0.1 on [0, 6] in each of its parameters, so the
capped family is searched over a 61 × 61 grid and each pure family over 61 points; the two con-
figurations at (p, h) = (19, 1) use step 0.01 on [0, 12], the gap there being the small quantity the
counterexample turns on.
A grid maximum lower-bounds the supremum of a family. Assessing separation also requires upper
bounds for the pure families to account for search resolution. On the witness instance we compute
these bounds by re-evaluating each pure family on a grid of step 0.002 over [0, 40], fifty times finer
and more than six times wider, which leaves both optima unchanged in value and in location. Since
the value is piecewise linear in the parameter, we estimate slope bounds by the largest slopes on that
grid: 26.76 for the base-stock family and 47.50 for the rate family. If these slope bounds are valid,
each supremum on [0, 40] is bounded by its grid maximum plus its estimated slope bound times half
a step, giving 11.940820 and 14.969375. Past the interval both curves fall away, being already below
−990 at 40 and below −2.6 × 107 at 106, as they must once ordering beyond demand buys only
holding cost. The best capped member attains 16.523438, giving a separation margin of 1.554062
against the bound. This numerical certificate uses slopes measured on the stated grid; the separation
is conditional on the validity of those estimated slope bounds. Its scope is numerical verification of
the witness instance.
C.3
RESULTS
Table 3 reports six configurations. The fourth row is the benchmark’s own lead-time support and is
the witness cited in Proposition 11: the best pure base-stock grid point attains 11.914062, the best
pure rate grid point 14.921875, and the capped member with θ = 2 and c = 1 attains 16.523438,
so the best grid point of K beats the best grid point of B ∪R by 1.601562, which is 3.20% of the
perfect-foresight revenue of 50 on that instance. This is the numerical strict-separation witness for
Proposition 11, under the slope-bound condition stated above.
The other five rows examine the conditions behind the gap. The first is a control: with support
{1, ∞} every surviving order lands exactly one period after it is placed, so two surviving orders
can never land in the same period and the lumping mechanism the design argument invokes is un-
available by construction. The separation gap there is exactly zero and the best capped member
only matches the pure rate optimum. The second row differs from it in the lead-time support alone,
holding the costs and the horizon fixed; admitting a second finite lead time opens the gap. This con-
trolled change provides evidence for the arrival-lumping mechanism. Across the five configurations
whose support contains two distinct finite lead times, so that a catch-up order and its successor can

D
CONSTRUCTION DETAILS OF THE POLICY LAYERS
This appendix gives the construction details needed to reproduce the layers in §3, following their
order in the main text.
D.1
THE THREE SLOTS
Table 4 names the three slots, gives the shipped setting of each, and identifies its author. We designed
the forecaster and the per-period arithmetic of the decision rules. The language model contributed a
mixture axis over the bank and a policy-family choice for the stochastic branch.
D.2
THE PREDICTIVE MODEL
One instantiation of the bank M holds nine members: the mean of the whole history; three expo-
nentially weighted moving averages with different smoothing constants; a Holt linear-trend member;
two rolling-window means; an AR(1) fitted by the sample lag-one autocorrelation; and a seasonal
member whose period is picked online by autocorrelation and re-picked as history accumulates.
Each member uses fixed configuration constants and is refit on the full history each period. Member

D.3
THE SHAPE LAYER
Variant g deseasonalizes by ηg = ηαg, renormalized to mean one, and runs a private copy of the
bank on dt/ηg[t]. Its weight is updated by the discounted predictive likelihood of §3.3,

with ˜pg the variant’s own model-averaged scoring density in deseasonalized space and the factor
